Beryllium's 2s electrons drop into the unshielded 1s shell upon ionization.
questions.explanation: Boron opens the higher-energy $$2p$$ subshell, which penetrates less deeply toward the nucleus than $$2s$$ and experiences substantial screening from both $$1s^2$$ and $$2s^2$$ electrons.

questions.prompt: When a ground-state boron atom ($$1s^2 2s^2 2p^1$$) undergoes first ionization to form $$\text{B}^+(g)$$, what is the electron configuration of the resulting cation?
questions.explanation: First ionization removes the highest-energy, loosest electron—boron's single $$2p^1$$ electron—leaving behind the closed-subshell $$1s^2 2s^2$$ configuration.

chunks.title: Orbital Crowding Explains the N-to-O Dip
chunks.content_markdown:
Now let's tackle the second zigzag, from nitrogen ($$Z = 7$$, $$1s^2 2s^2 2p^3$$, $$1402\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) to oxygen ($$Z = 8$$, $$1s^2 2s^2 2p^4$$, $$1314\,\text{kJ/mol}$$). Here *both* atoms lose a $$2p$$ electron, so $$2s$$-versus-$$2p$$ penetration cannot explain the drop! Instead, picture three empty two-seat train compartments representing the $$2p_x$$, $$2p_y$$, and $$2p_z$$ orbitals. By **Hund's Rule** (from Part 1), nitrogen's three $$2p$$ electrons each claim their own separate compartment with parallel spins ($$\uparrow\,\uparrow\,\uparrow$$).

Step one element right to oxygen ($$2p^4$$), and the fourth passenger *must* squeeze into an already occupied compartment ($$\uparrow\downarrow\,\uparrow\,\uparrow$$)! Sharing the exact same spatial orbital brings two negatively charged electrons much closer together, creating extra Coulombic pushback. That **spin-pairing repulsion dip (N/O anomaly)** gives oxygen's paired $$2p$$ electron an energetic boost out the door, trimming $$IE_1$$ by $$88\,\text{kJ/mol}$$!

questions.prompt: Why is oxygen's first ionization energy ($$1314\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) slightly lower than nitrogen's ($$1402\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) even though oxygen has a higher nuclear charge?
choices: Oxygen's eighth electron enters the 3s subshell rather than staying in 2p.
Repulsion between two spin-paired electrons in one 2p orbital eases removal.
Nitrogen's three 2p electrons all pair together inside a single low-energy 2p_x orbital.
Oxygen's inner 1s core expands outward and shields the 2p shell completely.
questions.explanation: In oxygen's $$2p^4$$ subshell, one $$2p$$ orbital holds a spin-paired electron duo whose close-range interelectronic repulsion raises the electron's energy and makes it easier to remove.

questions.prompt: Once fluorine ($$Z = 9$$, $$2p^5$$) follows oxygen across Period 2, what happens to $$IE_1$$—and why?
choices: It rises sharply to 1681 kJ/mol because climbing Z_eff outweighs pairing repulsion.
It drops further to 1100 kJ/mol because fluorine contains two spin-paired 2p orbitals.
It stays identical to oxygen's value because all 2p orbitals have equal energy.
It drops below boron's value because five 2p electrons shield each other completely.
questions.explanation: Oxygen already paid the initial spin-pairing jump at $$2p^4$$; stepping right to fluorine adds another $$+0.65$$ boost in $$Z_{\text{eff}}$$, sending $$IE_1$$ back onto its steep upward climb ($$1681\,\text{kJ/mol}$$).

chunks.title: Period 3 Echoes and Demystifying Half-Filled Subshells
chunks.content_markdown:
A great scientific explanation doesn't just patch one row—it predicts the next row too! Drop down to Period 3 and check the lab numbers: Group 2 magnesium ($$3s^2$$, $$738\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) dips right on cue at Group 13 aluminum ($$3s^2 3p^1$$, $$578\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) as the $$3p$$ subshell opens, and Group 15 phosphorus ($$3p^3$$, $$1012\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) dips slightly at Group 16 sulfur ($$3p^4$$, $$1000\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) the instant $$3p$$ spin pairing begins!

Chemists often refer to the local ionization peak at $$np^3$$ (like nitrogen and phosphorus) as **half-filled subshell stability**. Just keep your feet planted on solid physics: a half-filled $$np^3$$ subshell isn't blessed by mystical "symmetry magic"! Rather, up through $$np^3$$ every added electron enjoys its own separate orbital while $$Z_{\text{eff}}$$ climbs—and parallel-spin electrons naturally steer clear of one another through quantum wave symmetry—whereas $$np^4$$ abruptly incurs same-orbital pairing repulsion.

questions.prompt: Which pair of Period 3 neighbors reproduces the exact same spin-pairing ionization dip seen between nitrogen and oxygen in Period 2?
choices: Sodium ($$Z = 11$$) and magnesium ($$Z = 12$$)
Magnesium ($$Z = 12$$) and aluminum ($$Z = 13$$)
Silicon ($$Z = 14$$) and phosphorus ($$Z = 15$$)
Phosphorus ($$Z = 15$$) and sulfur ($$Z = 16$$)
questions.explanation: Phosphorus ($$[\text{Ne}]\,3s^2 3p^3$$) has three singly occupied $$3p$$ orbitals, whereas sulfur ($$[\text{Ne}]\,3s^2 3p^4$$) forces two electrons to pair in one $$3p$$ orbital, causing $$IE_1$$ to dip from $$1012$$ to $$1000\,\text{kJ/mol}$$.

questions.prompt: Which ordering accurately places the four Period 2 elements beryllium ($$\text{Be}$$), boron ($$\text{B}$$), nitrogen ($$\text{N}$$), and oxygen ($$\text{O}$$) in order of *increasing* $$IE_1$$?
choices: $$\text{Be} < \text{B} < \text{N} < \text{O}$$
$$\text{B} < \text{Be} < \text{N} < \text{O}$$
$$\text{B} < \text{Be} < \text{O} < \text{N}$$
$$\text{Be} < \text{B} < \text{O} < \text{N}$$
questions.explanation: Because both subshell dips invert adjacent pairs ($$\text{B} < \text{Be}$$ at $$801 < 900\,\text{kJ/mol}$$ and $$\text{O} < \text{N}$$ at $$1314 < 1402\,\text{kJ/mol}$$), the true increasing order is $$\text{B} < \text{Be} < \text{O} < \text{N}$$.

chunks.title: X-Raying Aufbau—and Asking What Comes After IE_1
chunks.content_markdown:
Pause to admire how Period 2's eight ionization numbers—$$\text{Li} < \text{B} < \text{Be} < \text{C} < \text{O} < \text{N} < \text{F} < \text{Ne}$$—tell the entire quantum story of the $$n = 2$$ shell in a single breath! Rising $$Z_{\text{eff}}$$ sets the steep upward slope, the $$2s \to 2p$$ penetration boundary leaves its notch at boron, and Hund's rule leaves its notch at oxygen.

Until now, though, we have stopped our experiment the moment a *single* electron came off. In real chemistry, magnesium routinely surrenders *two* electrons to form $$\text{Mg}^{2+}$$ and aluminum surrenders *three* to form $$\text{Al}^{3+}$$, yet sodium flatly refuses to form $$\text{Na}^{2+}$$ in any ordinary compound! What happens to the energy price tag when we come back with tweezers for a second, third, or fourth electron from the very same atom? Let's find out in Section 8.

questions.prompt: Across all eight elements of Period 2, which complete ranking lists first ionization energy $$IE_1$$ strictly from *lowest* to *highest*?
choices: $$\text{Li} < \text{Be} < \text{B} < \text{C} < \text{N} < \text{O} < \text{F} < \text{Ne}$$
$$\text{Li} < \text{B} < \text{Be} < \text{C} < \text{O} < \text{N} < \text{F} < \text{Ne}$$
$$\text{B} < \text{Li} < \text{Be} < \text{C} < \text{N} < \text{O} < \text{F} < \text{Ne}$$
$$\text{Li} < \text{B} < \text{C} < \text{Be} < \text{O} < \text{F} < \text{N} < \text{Ne}$$
questions.explanation: Starting from $$\text{Li}$$ and ascending to $$\text{Ne}$$, the two one-step inversions swap $$\text{Be}/\text{B}$$ and $$\text{N}/\text{O}$$, producing $$\text{Li} < \text{B} < \text{Be} < \text{C} < \text{O} < \text{N} < \text{F} < \text{Ne}$$.

questions.prompt: Why does sulfur's spin-pairing dip below phosphorus in Period 3 ($$1000$$ vs. $$1012\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) measure smaller than oxygen's dip below nitrogen in Period 2 ($$1314$$ vs. $$1402\,\text{kJ/mol}$$)?
choices: Larger 3p orbitals give paired electrons more room, softening their repulsion.
Sulfur places paired electrons into separate 3d orbitals instead of one 3p orbital.
Phosphorus already holds two spin-paired 3p orbitals in its neutral ground state.
Period 3 nuclei exert weaker valence Z_eff than corresponding Period 2 nuclei.
questions.explanation: Because $$n = 3$$ orbitals are spatially larger and more diffuse than compact $$n = 2$$ orbitals, two electrons paired inside a $$3p$$ orbital stay slightly farther apart on average and repel less fiercely.

sections.title: 8. Successive Ionization Energies and the Core-Electron Cliff
sections.summary: What happens if we keep plucking a second, third, or fourth electron from the same atom? Across five conversational chunks, learners see why successive ionization energies always climb (IE_1 < IE_2 < IE_3) as positive charge builds, encounter the massive core-electron ionization cliff when stripping breaches a closed noble-gas shell, use step-jump tables to deduce an unknown element's group and valence count, connect the cliff to stable main-group ion charges, and see why transition metals always lose outer ns electrons before (n-1)d electrons.

chunks.title: Why Sodium Stops at +1 While Magnesium Stops at +2
chunks.content_markdown:
Open your kitchen pantry or medicine cabinet and check the mineral labels: table salt always carries $$\text{Na}^+$$, Epsom salt always carries $$\text{Mg}^{2+}$$, and antiperspirant alum always carries $$\text{Al}^{3+}$$. Yet nowhere in nature will you ever stumble across an ordinary compound built from $$\text{Na}^{2+}$$ or $$\text{Mg}^{3+}$$! Why does every main-group metal obey such a strict ceiling on how many electrons it gives up?

To uncover that ceiling experimentally, chemists measure **successive ionization energies ($$IE_2, IE_3, \dots$$)**—the energy needed to remove a second, third, or fourth electron sequentially from a single gas-phase particle. While $$IE_1$$ strips a neutral atom $$\text{X}(g)$$, the second ionization energy $$IE_2$$ removes an electron from the singly charged cation:

$$\text{X}^+(g) \to \text{X}^{2+}(g) + e^-$$

Similarly, $$IE_3$$ strips $$\text{X}^{2+}(g)$$ to form $$\text{X}^{3+}(g)$$, one electron at a time.

questions.prompt: Which gas-phase chemical equation defines the *third* ionization energy ($$IE_3$$) of aluminum?
choices: $$\text{Al}(g) \to \text{Al}^{3+}(g) + 3e^-$$
questions.explanation: Each successive ionization energy removes just *one* electron from the previous ion; thus $$IE_3$$ removes a single electron from $$\text{Al}^{2+}(g)$$ to yield $$\text{Al}^{3+}(g)$$.

questions.prompt: How is the total energy required to convert $$\text{Mg}(g)$$ completely into $$\text{Mg}^{2+}(g) + 2e^-$$ related to magnesium's individual ionization steps?
choices: It equals the arithmetic sum $$IE_1 + IE_2$$.
It equals the second ionization energy $$IE_2$$ alone.
It equals the difference $$IE_2 - IE_1$$ between steps.
It equals twice the first ionization energy $$2 \times IE_1$$.
questions.explanation: Stripping two electrons from neutral $$\text{Mg}(g)$$ proceeds through removing the first electron ($$IE_1$$) followed by removing the second from $$\text{Mg}^+(g)$$ ($$IE_2$$), requiring $$IE_1 + IE_2$$ in total.

chunks.title: Rising Prices—and the Core-Electron Ionization Cliff
chunks.content_markdown:
First, notice a rock-solid rule that holds for *every* element on the periodic table: $$IE_1 < IE_2 < IE_3 < IE_4$$. Even when two electrons leave the exact same subshell—like magnesium's two $$3s^2$$ electrons ($$IE_1 = 738\,\text{kJ/mol}$$, $$IE_2 = 1451\,\text{kJ/mol}$$)—removing the second electron roughly doubles in price because fewer remaining electrons repel each other inside a shrunken, positively charged $$\text{Mg}^+$$ ion.

Now watch what happens when we reach for magnesium's *third* electron! Instead of another gentle doubling to roughly $$2900\,\text{kJ/mol}$$, $$IE_3$$ explodes more than fivefold to a staggering $$7733\,\text{kJ/mol}$$! Why? Because $$\text{Mg}^{2+}$$ has completely emptied its $$n = 3$$ valence shell; the third electron must be torn out of the compact, weakly shielded $$n = 2$$ neon core! Chemists call that dramatic five-to-tenfold spike the **core-electron ionization cliff**.

questions.prompt: Why is $$IE_2$$ of magnesium ($$1451\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) nearly double $$IE_1$$ ($$738\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) even though both electrons come from the very same $$3s$$ orbital?
choices: Magnesium's remaining 3s electron drops into the empty 1s shell after IE_1.
Magnesium gains an extra nuclear proton as soon as its first electron departs.
Less electron repulsion shrinks Mg^+ and strengthens pull on electron two.
Spin-pairing repulsion inside Mg^+ pushes the second 3s electron closer to the core.
questions.explanation: Once the first $$3s$$ electron leaves, the remaining $$3s^1$$ electron no longer feels same-orbital repulsion and must be pulled away from a smaller, net-positive $$\text{Mg}^+$$ cation.

questions.prompt: What physical boundary causes sodium's second ionization energy ($$4562\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) to jump more than ninefold above its first ionization energy ($$496\,\text{kJ/mol}$$)?
choices: The second electron is pulled from a half-filled 3p^3 valence subshell.
The second electron must be removed from the inner n = 2 neon core shell.
Sodium's nucleus doubles its shielding constant sigma once 3s^1 is emptied.
Forming Na^2+ forces two inner core electrons to pair inside one 2s orbital.
questions.explanation: Neutral sodium is $$1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^1$$; after $$IE_1$$ removes the lone $$3s^1$$ valence electron, $$IE_2$$ must breach the closed $$n = 2$$ core, where $$n$$ is smaller and $$Z_{\text{eff}}$$ is much larger.

chunks.title: Detective Work with Unknown Ionization Tables
chunks.content_markdown:
Once you recognize the core-electron cliff, a table of successive ionization energies reads like an open ID card! Suppose a lab hands you an unknown Period 3 element whose first five ionization energies (in $$\text{kJ/mol}$$) read:

$$786 \;\to\; 1577 \;\to\; 3232 \;\to\; 4356 \;\to\; 16{,}091$$

Scan the ratios from step to step: the first four removals climb at a brisk, ordinary pace (roughly $$1.3\times$$ to $$2\times$$ per step), and then—*wham!*—$$IE_5$$ leaps nearly fourfold from $$4356$$ to $$16{,}091\,\text{kJ/mol}$$! That tells you immediately that four outer valence electrons came off before electron #5 hit the inner neon core, identifying our mystery atom as silicon ($$[\text{Ne}]\,3s^2 3p^2$$, Group 14)! And because ordinary chemical bonds release only a few hundred to a couple thousand $$\text{kJ/mol}$$, nature simply cannot pay the $$4562\,\text{kJ/mol}$$ surcharge for $$\text{Na}^{2+}$$ or the $$7733\,\text{kJ/mol}$$ surcharge for $$\text{Mg}^{3+}$$.

questions.prompt: An unknown Period 3 main-group element has successive ionization energies (in $$\text{kJ/mol}$$) of $$IE_1 = 578$$, $$IE_2 = 1817$$, $$IE_3 = 2745$$, and $$IE_4 = 11{,}577$$. Which element is it?
choices: Sodium (Group 1, $$3s^1$$)
Magnesium (Group 2, $$3s^2$$)
Silicon (Group 14, $$3s^2 3p^2$$)
Aluminum (Group 13, $$3s^2 3p^1$$)
questions.explanation: Three valence electrons are removed at moderate cost before the massive core-electron cliff between $$IE_3$$ ($$2745$$) and $$IE_4$$ ($$11{,}577\,\text{kJ/mol}$$), identifying a $$3$$-valence-electron Group 13 atom: aluminum.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't solid sodium chloride form with the formula $$\text{NaCl}_2$$ (containing $$\text{Na}^{2+}$$ ions) even though $$\text{Na}^{2+}$$ would attract two chloride anions?
choices: Crystal attraction cannot repay the huge 4562 kJ/mol core cost of IE_2.
Chlorine atoms refuse to accept electrons whenever 2+ cations are nearby.
Removing a second electron from sodium is exothermic and melts the salt crystal.
Sodium nuclei contain only one positively charged proton available for ionic bonding.
questions.explanation: Breaching sodium's $$n = 2$$ neon core at $$IE_2 = 4562\,\text{kJ/mol}$$ demands far more energy than extra crystal lattice attractions can ever pay back.

chunks.title: The Transition-Metal Twist: Lose ns Before (n-1)d!
chunks.content_markdown:
Ready for one of chemistry's favorite plot twists? Recall from Part 1's Madelung $$(n + l)$$ building-up rule that neutral iron ($$Z = 26$$) fills $$4s$$ before $$3d$$, giving configuration $$[\text{Ar}]\,4s^2 3d^6$$. Naturally, almost every student guesses that ionizing iron to $$\text{Fe}^{2+}$$ strips out two "last-in" $$3d$$ electrons. Magnetic and spectroscopic tests prove the exact opposite!

Every transition metal obeys the **ns-before-(n-1)d cation rule**: when a $$d$$-block atom loses electrons to form a cation, electrons ALWAYS depart from the outer $$ns$$ subshell *before* the inner $$(n - 1)d$$ subshell! Thus $$\text{Fe}^{2+}$$ has configuration $$[\text{Ar}]\,3d^6$$ (zero $$4s$$ electrons left!), and $$\text{Fe}^{3+}$$ is $$[\text{Ar}]\,3d^5$$. Once $$3d$$ orbitals begin filling in a transition metal, compact $$3d$$ waves experience stronger nuclear attraction and settle slightly below the spatially outer $$4s$$ shell, leaving $$4s$$ electrons on the exposed frontier.

questions.prompt: Neutral manganese ($$Z = 25$$) has ground-state configuration $$[\text{Ar}]\,4s^2 3d^5$$. What is the ground-state electron configuration of the $$\text{Mn}^{2+}$$ cation?
questions.explanation: By the $$ns$$-before-$$(n-1)d$$ cation rule, forming $$\text{Mn}^{2+}$$ removes both outer $$4s^2$$ electrons first, leaving behind the half-filled $$[\text{Ar}]\,3d^5$$ configuration.

questions.prompt: When neutral zinc ($$Z = 30$$, $$[\text{Ar}]\,4s^2 3d^{10}$$) loses two electrons to form $$\text{Zn}^{2+}$$, which orbitals lose those two electrons?
choices: Both electrons depart from the spatially outer 4s orbital.
Both electrons depart from the inner 3d subshell.
One electron departs from 4s and one departs from 3d.
Both electrons depart from the argon core's 3p subshell.
questions.explanation: All d-block atoms strip outer $$4s$$ electrons before $$3d$$ electrons, giving $$\text{Zn}^{2+}$$ the closed-subshell configuration $$[\text{Ar}]\,3d^{10}$$.

chunks.title: Why Iron Wears Two Charges—and Flipping to Electron Gain
chunks.content_markdown:
Look how the $$ns$$-before-$$(n-1)d$$ rule and successive ionization energies explain another everyday observation: unlike sodium (strictly $$+1$$) or magnesium (strictly $$+2$$), transition metals like iron effortlessly form *multiple* familiar ions such as green $$\text{Fe}^{2+}$$ and rust-red $$\text{Fe}^{3+}$$! Because outer $$4s$$ and inner $$3d$$ energies sit relatively close together—and neither crosses into the deep $$[\text{Ar}]$$ core—removing a third electron from $$\text{Fe}^{2+}$$ ($$[\text{Ar}]\,3d^6 \to [\text{Ar}]\,3d^5$$, aided by shedding $$3d$$ spin-pairing repulsion!) rises smoothly without hitting a core cliff.

Across Sections 6, 7, and 8, we have explored every angle of prying electrons *off* an atom. Now let's turn the entire experiment inside out! Instead of pulling an electron away, what happens energetically when we hand a brand-new electron *to* a neutral gas-phase atom? Let's meet electron affinity in Section 9.

questions.prompt: Why can transition metals like iron and copper commonly form several stable cation charges (such as $$\text{Fe}^{2+}$$ and $$\text{Fe}^{3+}$$), whereas magnesium forms only $$\text{Mg}^{2+}$$?
choices: Transition metals lack inner noble-gas cores, so ionization energies decrease at higher charges.
Close ns and (n-1)d energies allow multiple removals before hitting the core cliff.
Magnesium's 3s electrons sit deeper inside the nucleus than iron's 1s core electrons.
Transition metals gain nuclear neutrons that neutralize extra positive charge during reactions.
questions.explanation: After a transition metal loses its outer $$ns$$ electrons, additional $$(n-1)d$$ electrons sit fairly close in energy without breaching the noble-gas core, avoiding an insurmountable cliff.

questions.prompt: Between which two ionization steps would titanium ($$Z = 22$$, configuration $$[\text{Ar}]\,4s^2 3d^2$$) encounter its massive argon-core ionization cliff?
choices: Between $$IE_1$$ and $$IE_2$$
Between $$IE_2$$ and $$IE_3$$
Between $$IE_3$$ and $$IE_4$$
Between $$IE_4$$ and $$IE_5$$
questions.explanation: Titanium has four removable outer electrons outside its $$[\text{Ar}]$$ core (two $$4s$$ removed first, then two $$3d$$); removing a *fifth* electron ($$IE_5$$) must break into the closed $$[\text{Ar}]$$ core.

sections.title: 9. Electron Affinity and the Chlorine-Over-Fluorine Anomaly
sections.summary: Flipping ionization around, learners examine what happens energetically when a neutral gas-phase atom captures an extra electron. Across five chunks, they define electron affinity (EA) and relate it to anion detachment, untangle positive-affinity versus thermodynamic delta-E sign conventions, explain why halogens eagerly release energy while alkaline earths, Group 15 p^3 atoms, and noble gases resist attachment, trace diminishing affinity down heavier groups, and solve the famous Cl > F (and S > O) anomaly caused by fierce crowding inside tiny Period 2 2p orbitals.

chunks.title: Why Would a Neutral Atom Welcome a Negative Stranger?
chunks.content_markdown:
Pause and ponder a seeming paradox: a neutral chlorine atom already balances $$17$$ positive protons with $$17$$ negative electrons for an exact overall charge of zero. Drift a stray $$18$$th electron past that electrically neutral atom in a vacuum, and naive intuition says nothing should happen. Instead, the chlorine atom snaps that extra electron into its outer shell and releases $$349\,\text{kJ/mol}$$ of energy—more energy per mole than exploding hydrogen-oxygen rocket fuel!

How can an overall neutral atom pull in a negatively charged guest so fiercely? Thank **incomplete same-shell shielding** once again! An electron approaching chlorine's open $$3p$$ slot doesn't see a canceled-out zero charge; it looks right past chlorine's side-by-side $$3s^2 3p^5$$ neighbors to feel a hefty positive $$Z_{\text{eff}}$$! Chemists measure this pull via **electron affinity ($$EA$$)**, tracking attachment of one electron to an isolated gas-phase atom:

$$\text{X}(g) + e^- \to \text{X}^-(g)$$

questions.prompt: What physical mechanism allows an electrically neutral atom like chlorine to attract and bind an additional negatively charged electron?
choices: Incomplete valence shielding leaves a strong positive Z_eff in the 3p shell.
Neutral chlorine atoms temporarily convert one core electron into a positively charged proton.
Gravitational attraction between the heavy nucleus and the incoming electron overcomes charge.
Outer 3p electrons migrate into the 1s shell to leave an unshielded +7 core behind.
questions.explanation: Because outer valence electrons shield each other incompletely, a vacant spot in the valence shell still experiences a strong net positive effective nuclear charge $$Z_{\text{eff}}$$.

questions.prompt: Which balanced gas-phase equation represents the electron-attachment process used to evaluate the electron affinity of oxygen?
choices: $$\text{O}(g) \to \text{O}^+(g) + e^-$$
$$\text{O}(g) + e^- \to \text{O}^-(g)$$
$$\text{O}^+(g) + e^- \to \text{O}(g)$$
questions.explanation: First electron affinity tracks a single isolated neutral gas-phase atom $$\text{O}(g)$$ capturing one electron to form the singly charged gaseous anion $$\text{O}^-(g)$$.

chunks.title: Untangling Electron Affinity Sign Conventions
chunks.content_markdown:
Before you ever open two different chemistry textbooks side by side, let's armor-plate you against a notorious notation quirk: **electron affinity sign conventions**. In standard heat-and-energy accounting (**thermodynamics**), an exothermic step that *releases* energy outward carries a **negative** reaction energy ($$\Delta E_{\text{ea}} = -349\,\text{kJ/mol}$$ for chlorine). Physics and spectroscopy reference tables, however, define **electron affinity ($$EA$$)** itself as the *positive amount of energy released* upon attachment—or equivalently, the endothermic energy required to pluck that extra electron back off the anion ($$\text{X}^-(g) \to \text{X}(g) + e^-$$), making chlorine's $$EA = +349\,\text{kJ/mol}$$ ($$+3.62\,\text{eV}$$).

Spot that neat insight: $$EA$$ of neutral $$\text{X}$$ is *not* the reverse of $$IE_1$$ of $$\text{X}$$ (which involves $$\text{X}^+$$); rather, $$EA$$ of $$\text{X}$$ equals the ionization energy of the *anion* $$\text{X}^-$$! Under the standard $$EA$$ convention, a **larger positive $$EA$$** (more negative $$\Delta E_{\text{ea}}$$) signals a stronger appetite for an extra electron.

questions.prompt: When a gas-phase bromine atom captures an electron exothermically, releasing $$325\,\text{kJ/mol}$$ of energy, how are $$EA$$ and the thermodynamic energy change $$\Delta E_{\text{ea}}$$ written?
choices: $$EA = -325\,\text{kJ/mol}$$ and $$\Delta E_{\text{ea}} = +325\,\text{kJ/mol}$$
$$EA = +325\,\text{kJ/mol}$$ and $$\Delta E_{\text{ea}} = -325\,\text{kJ/mol}$$
$$EA = +325\,\text{kJ/mol}$$ and $$\Delta E_{\text{ea}} = +325\,\text{kJ/mol}$$
$$EA = 0\,\text{kJ/mol}$$ and $$\Delta E_{\text{ea}} = -325\,\text{kJ/mol}$$
questions.explanation: Exothermic electron capture releases energy, corresponding to a negative thermodynamic reaction energy ($$\Delta E_{\text{ea}} = -325\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) and a positive electron affinity value ($$EA = +325\,\text{kJ/mol}$$).

questions.prompt: Measuring the positive electron affinity $$EA$$ of a neutral fluorine atom $$\text{F}(g)$$ is energetically identical to measuring the minimum energy required for which reverse step?
choices: $$\text{F}(g) \to \text{F}^+(g) + e^-$$
$$\text{F}_2(g) \to 2\text{F}(g)$$
$$\text{F}^-(g) \to \text{F}(g) + e^-$$
questions.explanation: Reversing $$\text{F}(g) + e^- \to \text{F}^-(g)$$ detaches the extra electron from the fluoride anion $$\text{F}^-(g)$$ back to neutral $$\text{F}(g) + e^-$$, requiring an energy input equal to $$EA$$.

chunks.title: Halogen Feasts and Three Subshell Roadblocks
chunks.content_markdown:
Across a period from left to right, rising $$Z_{\text{eff}}$$ generally increases an atom's welcome for an extra electron, culminating in the **Group 17 halogens** ($$ns^2 np^5$$), which release more energy than any other family as the incoming electron completes a tightly pulled $$np^6$$ subshell.

Along each row, however, three dramatic subshell roadblocks drive $$EA$$ down near zero or even *negative* (meaning $$\Delta E_{\text{ea}} > 0$$, so an isolated anion is unstable and spits the electron right back out!). First, **Group 18 noble gases** ($$np^6$$, like neon and argon) must exile any incoming electron to a brand-new $$n + 1$$ shell outside a closed core. Second, **Group 2 alkaline earths** ($$ns^2$$, like beryllium and magnesium) must place a newcomer into a higher-energy, core-shielded $$np$$ subshell. Third, **Group 15 nitrogen** ($$2p^3$$) balks because adding a fourth $$2p$$ electron forces spin pairing inside an already occupied orbital!

questions.prompt: Why do noble gases like neon and argon exhibit negative electron affinities (endothermic $$\Delta E_{\text{ea}} > 0$$), refusing to form stable gas-phase anions?
choices: Added electrons must enter the next shell n + 1 outside a full core.
Noble-gas nuclei contain zero unshielded protons once the np^6 subshell is filled.
Incoming electrons must pair inside the innermost 1s orbital, violating Pauli exclusion.
Halogens steal electrons away even inside a pure sample of isolated neon gas.
questions.explanation: With its $$ns^2 np^6$$ valence shell completely full, a noble gas can accommodate an extra electron only in the higher-energy $$(n + 1)s$$ orbital, where heavy core screening leaves no net binding.

questions.prompt: Why does carbon ($$2p^2$$, $$EA = +122\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) release substantial energy upon capturing an electron, whereas next-door nitrogen ($$2p^3$$, $$EA \approx -7\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) resists capturing one?
choices: Carbon places the added electron in 2s, whereas nitrogen must place it in 3s.
Carbon fills an empty 2p orbital, while nitrogen must spin-pair in 2p.
Nitrogen has a smaller effective nuclear charge Z_eff on its 2p subshell than carbon.
Carbon loses a proton during attachment, whereas nitrogen retains all seven protons.
questions.explanation: Carbon ($$2p_x^1 2p_y^1$$) welcomes a third electron into its empty $$2p_z$$ orbital without pairing, whereas half-filled nitrogen ($$2p_x^1 2p_y^1 2p_z^1$$) incurs close-range spin-pairing repulsion.

chunks.title: The Famous Chlorine-Over-Fluorine Anomaly
chunks.content_markdown:
Pop quiz: which element on the entire periodic table boasts the highest electron affinity? Nine out of ten chemistry students guess **fluorine**—after all, fluorine sits at the top of Group 17 with the smallest halogen radius! Check the lab measurements, however, and **chlorine takes the crown**: chlorine releases $$349\,\text{kJ/mol}$$ ($$3.62\,\text{eV}$$), noticeably beating fluorine's $$328\,\text{kJ/mol}$$ ($$3.40\,\text{eV}$$)! Even in Group 16 next door, Period 3 sulfur ($$200\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) handily beats Period 2 oxygen ($$141\,\text{kJ/mol}$$).

What explains this **Period 2 compact-shell anomaly (Cl > F)**? Picture squeezing one extra passenger into a tiny two-seat subcompact car ($$2p$$) versus a roomy van ($$3p$$). Fluorine's $$n = 2$$ valence shell is *so* tiny and densely packed with seven valence electrons that shoehorning an eighth electron into that cramped space triggers intense close-range electron-electron repulsion—shaving roughly $$21\,\text{kJ/mol}$$ off fluorine's energy payoff!

questions.prompt: Why does chlorine ($$EA = +349\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) release *more* energy upon capturing an electron than fluorine ($$EA = +328\,\text{kJ/mol}$$)?
choices: Chlorine has a smaller covalent radius that pulls the incoming electron closer to the nucleus.
Fluorine must place an incoming eighth valence electron into the empty 3s orbital.
Strong repulsion inside fluorine's tiny 2p shell offsets part of its pull.
Chlorine uses empty 3d orbitals to eliminate all core shielding from its neon inner shell.
questions.explanation: Fluorine's ultra-compact $$2p$$ subshell packs high electron density into a tiny volume, so adding an extra electron creates strong interelectronic repulsion compared to chlorine's roomier $$3p$$ subshell.

questions.prompt: Combining the Period 2 compact-shell anomaly with the normal distance trend below Period 3, which ranking orders the four common halogens from *highest* to *lowest* electron affinity $$EA$$?
choices: $$\text{F} > \text{Cl} > \text{Br} > \text{I}$$
$$\text{I} > \text{Br} > \text{Cl} > \text{F}$$
$$\text{Cl} > \text{Br} > \text{F} > \text{I}$$
$$\text{Cl} > \text{F} > \text{Br} > \text{I}$$
questions.explanation: Chlorine ($$349\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) beats compact fluorine ($$328\,\text{kJ/mol}$$), followed closely by bromine ($$325\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) and then iodine ($$295\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) as increasing shell distance $$n$$ weakens attraction: $$\text{Cl} > \text{F} > \text{Br} > \text{I}$$.

chunks.title: Chlorine's Goldilocks Shell—and Moving Inside Real Bonds
chunks.content_markdown:
Period 3 turns out to be the "Goldilocks sweet spot" for capturing an extra electron across all nonmetal groups: a $$3p$$ orbital sits close enough to the nucleus to feel brisk $$Z_{\text{eff}}$$, yet offers enough elbow room to avoid Period 2's $$2p$$ traffic jam! Below Period 3—from chlorine ($$349\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) to bromine ($$325\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) to iodine ($$295\,\text{kJ/mol}$$), and from sulfur to selenium to tellurium—increasing principal shell distance $$n$$ resumes command and $$EA$$ tapers gently downward.

Notice one last crucial detail before our grand finale: even when neutral oxygen exothermically grabs *one* electron ($$EA_1 = +141\,\text{kJ/mol}$$), forcing a *second* negative electron onto an already negative $$\text{O}^-(g)$$ ion to make $$\text{O}^{2-}(g)$$ is fiercely endothermic (requiring $$+744\,\text{kJ/mol}$$ because two negative charges repel!). Isolated atoms only tell half the story. In Section 10, let's bring atoms *together* inside real chemical bonds through **electronegativity**.

questions.prompt: Following the exact same Period 2-versus-Period 3 pattern seen in the halogens, which Group 16 element has the *most positive* first electron affinity $$EA$$?
choices: Oxygen ($$Z = 8$$, Period 2)
Sulfur ($$Z = 16$$, Period 3)
Selenium ($$Z = 34$$, Period 4)
Tellurium ($$Z = 52$$, Period 5)
questions.explanation: Just as chlorine beats compact fluorine in Group 17, Period 3 sulfur ($$EA = +200\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) beats compact Period 2 oxygen ($$+141\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) and also beats larger heavier chalcogens below it.

questions.prompt: Why is adding a *second* electron to gas-phase $$\text{O}^-(g)$$ to form $$\text{O}^{2-}(g)$$ strongly endothermic even though $$\text{O}^{2-}$$ achieves a closed neon-like $$2p^6$$ shell?
choices: Adding a negative electron to negative O^- faces strong Coulomb repulsion.
The second electron must enter oxygen's empty 3s shell rather than completing the 2p subshell.
Gaining a second electron strips two protons out of the oxygen nucleus in the gas phase.
Spin pairing is forbidden by Pauli exclusion whenever a sixth electron enters a 2p subshell.
questions.explanation: Like charges repel: forcing a negatively charged $$e^-$$ onto a negatively charged $$\text{O}^-(g)$$ ion requires hefty external work in the gas phase (paid back in solids like $$\text{MgO}$$ by strong crystal lattice attractions).

sections.title: 10. Pauling vs. Mulliken Electronegativity and the Periodic Big Picture
sections.summary: In the capstone section, isolated-atom properties come together inside real chemical bonds through electronegativity. Learners define electronegativity (chi) and bond polarity from first principles, explore Linus Pauling's thermochemical scale built from extra heteronuclear bond strength, contrast it with Robert Mulliken's first-principles average of ionization energy and electron affinity, compare both scales across the table (including why light noble gases lack classical Pauling values), and synthesize how n and Z_eff unify every periodic trend and preview chemical bonding.

chunks.title: Tug-of-War Inside a Bond: Electronegativity and Polarity
chunks.content_markdown:
Inside a hydrogen gas molecule ($$\text{H–H}$$), two identical nuclei pull with equal strength on their shared pair of bonding electrons, keeping the electron cloud balanced symmetrically in the middle. Replace one hydrogen with fluorine to make hydrogen fluoride ($$\text{H–F}$$), however, and the shared cloud surges lopsidedly toward fluorine—draping fluorine in a partial negative charge ($$\delta-$$) and leaving hydrogen with a partial positive charge ($$\delta+$$)!

Chemists call that lopsided charge sharing **bond polarity** (forming a **polar covalent** bond), and they attribute it to **electronegativity** (written with the Greek letter chi, $$\chi$$): the ability of an atom *within a molecule* to attract shared bonding electrons toward itself. Whereas $$IE_1$$ and $$EA$$ clock isolated gas atoms gaining or losing whole electrons, electronegativity scores a tug-of-war *inside* a chemical bond!

questions.prompt: How does electronegativity ($$\chi$$) fundamentally differ from first ionization energy ($$IE_1$$) and electron affinity ($$EA$$)?
choices: Electronegativity scores shared-bond pull rather than isolated gas-atom transfers.
Electronegativity measures nuclear neutron-to-proton ratios rather than outer valence-shell attractions.
Electronegativity applies exclusively to pure metallic crystals rather than covalent molecules.
Electronegativity is measured directly in picometers by X-ray diffraction of frozen noble gases.
questions.explanation: Whereas $$IE_1$$ and $$EA$$ are directly measurable energies for complete electron loss or gain by an isolated gas-phase atom, $$\chi$$ quantifies an atom's pull on shared electrons within a chemical bond.

questions.prompt: In a polar covalent $$\text{H–Cl}$$ molecule where chlorine is significantly more electronegative than hydrogen, how is shared electron density distributed?
choices: Shared electrons sit exactly halfway between H and Cl, leaving zero partial charges.
Shared electrons shift toward H, giving hydrogen a partial negative charge ($$\delta-$$).
Shared electrons shift toward Cl, giving chlorine a partial negative charge ($$\delta-$$).
All eighteen electrons transfer onto H, creating an ionic $$\text{H}^-\text{Cl}^+$$ gas pair.
questions.explanation: More electronegative chlorine draws the shared bonding cloud closer to itself, acquiring a partial negative charge ($$\delta-$$) while leaving hydrogen partially positive ($$\delta+$$).

chunks.title: Linus Pauling's Clue: Bonus Strength in Mixed Bonds
chunks.content_markdown:
In $$1932$$, chemist Linus Pauling spotted an ingenious heat-of-reaction (**thermochemical**) clue hidden inside bond-breaking energies. Suppose an $$\text{H–F}$$ bond shared electrons just as evenly as $$\text{H–H}$$ ($$436\,\text{kJ/mol}$$) and $$\text{F–F}$$ ($$158\,\text{kJ/mol}$$); you would expect breaking $$\text{H–F}$$ to cost roughly their average, about $$297\,\text{kJ/mol}$$. Instead, snapping an $$\text{H–F}$$ bond in the lab demands a whopping $$568\,\text{kJ/mol}$$—an extra $$\Delta = 271\,\text{kJ/mol}$$ of bonus bond strength!

Pauling realized that whenever two partners pull unequally, the resulting $$\delta+$$ and $$\delta-$$ partial charges attract each other electrostatically, stiffening the bond! Setting the electronegativity gap proportional to the square root of that extra bond stabilization ($$|\chi_{\text{A}} - \chi_{\text{B}}| \propto \sqrt{\Delta}$$) and choosing hydrogen near $$2.20$$ as a reference anchor created the dimensionless **Pauling electronegativity scale**—stretching from cesium near $$0.79$$ at the bottom-left up to **fluorine at $$3.98$$** (famously rounded to $$4.0$$) at the top-right!

questions.prompt: What experimental data did Linus Pauling use in $$1932$$ to construct his original electronegativity scale?
choices: Covalent and van der Waals radii measured in frozen diatomic crystals
Bonus bond energy making A–B stronger than pure A–A and B–B bonds
Characteristic X-ray frequencies emitted when inner 1s core electrons are ejected
Successive core-electron ionization cliffs across Period 2 and Period 3 metals
questions.explanation: Pauling quantified how much stronger a mixed-element $$\text{A–B}$$ bond is than the expected average of pure $$\text{A–A}$$ and $$\text{B–B}$$ bonds, linking that extra ionic stabilization $$\Delta$$ to $$|\chi_{\text{A}} - \chi_{\text{B}}|$$.

questions.prompt: If two different nonmetals A and B turn out to have almost identical Pauling electronegativities ($$\chi_{\text{A}} \approx \chi_{\text{B}}$$), what does Pauling's model predict about the $$\text{A–B}$$ bond energy?
choices: The A–B bond will fail to form because identical electronegativities repel.
The A–B bond energy will be roughly triple the sum of A–A and B–B bond energies.
The A–B bond will be purely ionic with complete electron transfer from A to B.
The A–B bond energy will nearly match the average of A–A and B–B.
questions.explanation: When $$|\chi_{\text{A}} - \chi_{\text{B}}| \approx 0$$, the bond has negligible polarity ($$\Delta \approx 0$$), so its bond strength closely matches the nonpolar average of $$\text{A–A}$$ and $$\text{B–B}$$.

chunks.title: Robert Mulliken's Atomic Average: Hold Plus Grab
chunks.content_markdown:
Just two years after Pauling, physicist Robert S. Mulliken proposed a remarkably transparent alternative straight from isolated-atom physics. Imagine atoms $$\text{A}$$ and $$\text{B}$$ sharing a pair of electrons. For $$\text{A}$$ to win the tug-of-war, $$\text{A}$$ must simultaneously **grab** $$\text{B}$$'s electron strongly (high electron affinity $$EA$$) *and* **hold** onto its own electron stubbornly so $$\text{B}$$ cannot steal it (high ionization energy $$IE$$)!

Mulliken therefore defined **Mulliken electronegativity** ($$\chi_{\text{M}}$$) simply as the arithmetic average of an atom's ionization energy and electron affinity:

$$\chi_{\text{M}} = \frac{IE + EA}{2}$$

Watch how cleanly Mulliken's formula resolves our Section 9 cliffhanger between fluorine and chlorine! Although chlorine edges out fluorine slightly in $$EA$$ ($$3.62$$ vs. $$3.40\,\text{eV}$$), fluorine towers over chlorine in $$IE_1$$ ($$17.42$$ vs. $$12.97\,\text{eV}$$). Averaging the two gives fluorine $$10.41\,\text{eV}$$ versus chlorine's $$8.30\,\text{eV}$$—crowning **fluorine #1 in electronegativity** on both Pauling's and Mulliken's scales!

questions.prompt: Why did Robert Mulliken average *both* ionization energy and electron affinity—rather than using electron affinity alone—to define electronegativity?
choices: Bond tug-of-war requires attracting partner electrons while holding your own.
Ionization energy and electron affinity always have opposite signs that cancel core shielding.
Electron affinity can only be measured for alkali metals and never for nonmetals.
Averaging IE and EA eliminates principal quantum number n from periodic trends.
questions.explanation: In a shared bond between A and B, A pulls electron density toward itself by resisting loss of its own electron ($$\text{A} \to \text{A}^+$$, high $$IE$$) while welcoming extra density ($$\text{A} \to \text{A}^-$$, high $$EA$$).

questions.prompt: Why does fluorine outrank chlorine in electronegativity on both the Mulliken and Pauling scales even though chlorine has a slightly larger electron affinity $$EA$$?
choices: Fluorine has a much larger covalent radius that overlaps partner orbitals completely.
Chlorine has a negative first ionization energy that drags its Mulliken average down.
Fluorine's much higher ionization energy outweighs chlorine's small EA lead.
Pauling and Mulliken both excluded Period 3 elements when normalizing their scales.
questions.explanation: Fluorine's compact $$n = 2$$ shell gives it a huge advantage in ionization energy ($$17.42$$ vs. $$12.97\,\text{eV}$$) that easily swamps chlorine's small $$0.22\,\text{eV}$$ lead in electron affinity.

chunks.title: Comparing the Scales—and the Noble-Gas Blank Spot
chunks.content_markdown:
Plot Mulliken's atomic averages (in $$\text{eV}$$) against Pauling's bond-energy values across dozens of elements, and the two completely independent recipes fall along a striking straight line! Whether you measure reaction heat with Pauling or clock lone gas atoms in a spectrometer with Mulliken, electronegativity **climbs across periods from left to right** (rising $$Z_{\text{eff}}$$) and **decreases down groups from top to bottom** (expanding shell $$n$$), running from cesium ($$0.79$$) up to fluorine ($$3.98$$).

Comparing the two methods also solves a classic trivia stumper: why do standard Pauling charts leave helium and neon blank? Not because neon has "zero attraction" for electrons! Pauling's formula requires breaking real chemical bonds, and helium and neon form no stable ordinary compounds to measure! Heavier xenon *does* form bonds like $$\text{XeF}_2$$ (earning a hefty Pauling value near $$2.6$$), and Mulliken-style orbital scales confirm that neon's enormous $$IE_1$$ actually gives it fierce electron-holding power!

questions.prompt: Why are lighter noble gases such as helium and neon usually omitted or left blank on traditional Pauling electronegativity tables?
choices: Their effective nuclear charge Z_eff drops to zero once the outer shell closes.
Pauling's scale needs bond energies, and neither gas forms ordinary bonds.
Their first ionization energies are too small to register on spectroscopic instruments.
Helium and neon transfer all of their electrons to fluorine at room temperature.
questions.explanation: Because Pauling's thermochemical calculation extracts $$\chi$$ from measured mixed-element bond dissociation energies, elements that form no stable ordinary bonds lack classical Pauling inputs.

questions.prompt: Ordering oxygen ($$\text{O}$$), sulfur ($$\text{S}$$), silicon ($$\text{Si}$$), and sodium ($$\text{Na}$$) from *lowest* to *highest* electronegativity, which sequence is correct?
choices: $$\text{O} < \text{S} < \text{Si} < \text{Na}$$
$$\text{Na} < \text{S} < \text{Si} < \text{O}$$
$$\text{Si} < \text{Na} < \text{O} < \text{S}$$
$$\text{Na} < \text{Si} < \text{S} < \text{O}$$
questions.explanation: Electronegativity rises rightward across Period 3 ($$\text{Na} < \text{Si} < \text{S}$$) and climbs upward in Group 16 from Period 3 sulfur to Period 2 oxygen ($$\text{S} < \text{O}$$), yielding $$\text{Na} < \text{Si} < \text{S} < \text{O}$$.

chunks.title: One Electrostatic Map for All of Chemistry
chunks.content_markdown:
Step back and take in the view from the summit of Periodic Table Parts I and II! Every sweeping pattern we have traced—atomic and ionic radii, ionization sawtooths and subshell dips, core cliffs, electron affinities, and electronegativity—flows from just two master dials: **principal shell distance $$n$$** and **effective nuclear charge $$Z_{\text{eff}}$$**, sculpted in fine detail by orbital penetration and spin pairing.

March **up and right** toward fluorine, and shrinking $$n$$ plus surging $$Z_{\text{eff}}$$ contract the atom while driving $$IE_1$$, $$EA$$ (peaking at chlorine/fluorine), and $$\chi$$ skyward. March **down and left** toward cesium, and roomy shells loosen every grip. Best of all, pairing any two elements on our electronegativity map previews how matter bonds: two low-$$\chi$$ metals pool electrons in a **metallic** sea; two high-$$\chi$$ nonmetals share electrons in **covalent** molecules; and a low-$$\chi$$ metal meeting a high-$$\chi$$ nonmetal transfers electrons into an **ionic** crystal!

questions.prompt: Moving diagonally across the main-group periodic table from bottom-left cesium toward top-right fluorine, how do neutral atomic radius, $$IE_1$$, and electronegativity $$\chi$$ change overall?
choices: Atomic radius increases while both IE_1 and electronegativity decrease.
Atomic radius, IE_1, and electronegativity all increase together.
Atomic radius decreases while both IE_1 and electronegativity increase.
Atomic radius and IE_1 decrease while electronegativity remains constant.
questions.explanation: Moving upward lowers principal shell $$n$$ and moving rightward raises $$Z_{\text{eff}}$$; together they pull electron clouds tighter (smaller radius) and strengthen electron attraction (higher $$IE_1$$ and $$\chi$$).

questions.prompt: Using electronegativity trends, which pair of elements has the *largest* electronegativity difference $$|\chi_{\text{A}} - \chi_{\text{B}}|$$ and therefore forms the most strongly ionic bond?
choices: Carbon and sulfur
Cesium and fluorine
Lithium and iodine
Nitrogen and chlorine
questions.explanation: Pairing bottom-left cesium (lowest $$\chi \approx 0.79$$) with top-right fluorine (highest $$\chi \approx 3.98$$) maximizes $$|\chi_{\text{A}} - \chi_{\text{B}}|$$, driving complete electron transfer into ionic $$\text{Cs}^+\text{F}^-$$.
